Post to Discord whenever the Check Link module scans a link and finds it merely suspicious (not confirmed malicious, but worth a look).

Turn on/off checking how old a viewer's: Turn on/off checking how old a viewer's Twitch account is. Brand-new accounts are often throwaway bots, so this adds suspicion for very young accounts.

Only run the account age check on a user's very first message in chat.
Disable to check every message regardless of chat history
Turn on/off flagging messages that are m: Turn on/off flagging messages that are mostly (or entirely) spammed emotes.
Turn on/off flagging ALL-CAPS SPAM and r: Turn on/off flagging ALL-CAPS SPAM and repeated-character spam (like "AAAAAA" or "!!!!!!!").

Turn on/off flagging people for chatting too fast or repeating themselves. Covers two things:

Turn on/off the chat-wide protection layer.
While the filters above punish individual users, escalation watches the whole chat:
if many different users cause violations in a short time (a spam wave), a Twitch chat mode
like slow mode or follower-only is activated automatically to protect the entire chat.
The mode is chosen based on the dominant spam pattern of the wave:
Emote spam → slow > follow > sub (emote-only is excluded — it would legalize the spam)
Fresh accounts / message flooding → follow > sub > slow (locks out throwaway accounts entirely)
Caps/character spam → emote-only > slow > follow > sub (makes text spam impossible)
Only modes enabled below can be chosen — disabled modes fall through to the next preference
Step up the response if a spam wave cont:
Step up the response if a spam wave continues despite an active chat mode.
When the violation count is reached AGAIN while a mode is already running, the next suitable
mode from the preference list is activated on top of it.
(Example emote wave: 1st trigger = slow mode; spam continues, 2nd trigger = follower-only is added)
Disabled: repeated triggers only extend the duration of the already active mode
Always layer slow mode on top of whichev:
Always layer slow mode on top of whichever mode was auto-selected.
(Example: a fresh-account wave selects follower-only → slow mode is switched on as well,
so even users who pass the follow check can only post slowly)
Requires 'SlowMode Enabled'. Has no effect when slow mode itself is the chosen mode
Allow escalation to use Twitch slow mode:
Allow escalation to use Twitch slow mode.
Every user must wait between their own messages — spam gets massively throttled,
but nobody is locked out of chat. The gentlest mode and therefore the first choice
for emote waves and mixed spam patterns
Allow escalation to use follower-only mo:
Allow escalation to use follower-only mode.
Only users following the channel for at least 'Follow Age' can chat.
First choice against fresh-account waves and coordinated message flooding (bot attacks),
because throwaway accounts typically don't follow — the whole wave is locked out at once
while your regular viewers keep chatting normally
Allow escalation to use emote-only mode.
Only Twitch emotes can be posted — text messages become impossible, which stops
caps and character floods completely. First choice for caps waves,
but drastic for normal chatters: if it's too harsh for your community, leave it disabled
and slow mode takes over as the next preference.
Never chosen for emote spam or flood waves
Allow escalation to use subscriber-only:
Allow escalation to use subscriber-only mode.
Only subscribers (and mods/VIPs) can chat — effectively no spam bot ever passes,
but all non-subscribed viewers are silenced too. The most restrictive mode:
used as a last resort when better-fitting modes are disabled, or as the final step
of progressive escalation when a wave punches through everything else
Turn the whole Raid Protection module on: Turn the whole Raid Protection module on or off.

Reset the protection window to its full duration whenever a violation is detected.
Keeps the protection active as long as the spam wave continues
Allow raid protection to activate slow m:
Allow raid protection to activate slow mode.
Preferred response for emote spam waves and the general fallback for mixed patterns
Allow raid protection to activate follow:
Allow raid protection to activate follower-only mode.
Preferred response for coordinated message waves — raid bots follow right before spamming (or not at all),
so a follow-age requirement locks out the whole wave while established raiders can still chat
Allow raid protection to activate emote-:
Allow raid protection to activate emote-only mode.
Preferred response for caps/character floods, since text messages become impossible.
Never chosen for emote spam waves. If this is too drastic, disable it and slow mode takes over
Allow raid protection to activate subscr:
Allow raid protection to activate subscriber-only mode.
The most restrictive option — used as a last resort when better-fitting modes are disabled
Additionally layers slow mode on top of:
Additionally layers slow mode on top of whichever mode was auto-selected (requires SlowMode Enabled).
Has no effect when slow mode itself is the chosen mode
Activate a chat mode immediately when a:
Activate a chat mode immediately when a raid comes in, before any spam is detected.
Since no pattern data exists yet at that point, the mixed-pattern preference (slow > follow > sub > emote-only) is used.
Disabled: modes only activate once the first actual violation is registered, so friendly raids stay unrestricted
When a message contains a link, automati:
When a message contains a link, automatically run it through the Check Link module (a virus/phishing scanner) in the background.
This runs even for trusted roles like mods, VIPs, and subs — it's just a quiet safety check, not extra moderation on them.
Post a message in chat when a scanned li: Post a message in chat when a scanned link comes back clean/safe.
Post a message in chat when a scanned link comes back suspicious — not confirmed dangerous, but worth a second look.
Post a message in chat when a scanned link comes back confirmed malicious (viruses, phishing, etc.).
Post a message in chat if a link scan co: Post a message in chat if a link scan couldn't finish (the scanning service was slow or unavailable).
Turn the whole Twitch Warn module on or: Turn the whole Twitch Warn module on or off.
Also post a message in chat (in addition: Also post a message in chat (in addition to the warning screen the viewer sees) whenever a Twitch Warn is issued.
Turn on/off automatic escalation for rep:
Turn on/off automatic escalation for repeat offenders.
On: once a viewer has racked up enough warnings (set below), the next violation escalates straight to a timeout or ban instead of another warning.
Off: TwitchSentry just keeps issuing warnings and never escalates on its own.
When escalating, ban the viewer instead: When escalating, ban the viewer instead of the default timeout.
Post a message in chat when a moderator: Post a message in chat when a moderator grants or revokes a link permit.
Post a message in chat when a permit run: Post a message in chat when a permit runs out on its own (time expires without a moderator revoking it).
Let viewers redeem a Channel Points rewa: Let viewers redeem a Channel Points reward to grant themselves a temporary permit to post a link, without needing a moderator.
Double-check that @usernames mentioned i: Double-check that @usernames mentioned in a message actually exist on Twitch. Mentioning made-up/nonexistent users is a common bot-spam trick, so this adds extra suspicion when it happens.
Catch messages that use fancy/lookalike: Catch messages that use fancy/lookalike Unicode letters to sneak spam words past normal text matching (e.g. "Viewe𝗿𝘀 𝗌𝗍𝗋ea𝗆𝖻𝗈𝗈" instead of "Viewers streamboo").
Catch links that have spaces or dots add: Catch links that have spaces or dots added to dodge link detection (e.g. "twitch. tv" or "example . com" instead of a normal link).
Catch messages containing gift-code/vouc: Catch messages containing gift-code/voucher-code-looking strings (e.g. "GVP-8IJN-VV65-8QWG"), a common "free viewers" scam pattern.
Turn the whole Spam Learner module on or: Turn the whole Spam Learner module on or off. When off, it won't automatically suggest or add any new spam words — you'd only be protected by the keywords/patterns you've entered yourself.
Post a message in chat when the learner: Post a message in chat when the learner writes new suggestions or promotes something automatically.
Let the learner move well-proven suggest:
Let the learner move well-proven suggestions straight into the active rule list (spam.json) on its own, without needing your approval.
New finds always start as pending suggestions first — they only reach "trusted" and get auto-promoted once they've built up enough of a track record (the thresholds below control exactly how much).
Turn on/off automatic cleanup of old, no:
Turn on/off automatic cleanup of old, no-longer-relevant learner data.
When on, both active spam rules and pending suggestions are checked against recent chat history, and get removed if they've stopped showing up.
Keep entries you added to spam.json BY H:
Keep entries you added to spam.json BY HAND (marked with a "!" at the start) safe from automatic cleanup, even while decay is on.
Only turn this off if you want decay allowed to remove absolutely everything, including rules you wrote yourself.
Turn the whole AutoMod module on or off.
Also let TwitchSentry automatically appr: Also let TwitchSentry automatically approve/deny AutoMod-held messages that come from Twitch-restricted/monitored users (accounts Twitch itself is already keeping an eye on).
Turn the whole Check Link module on or o: Turn the whole Check Link module on or off.
Let moderators check a link by whisperin:
Let moderators check a link by whispering (DMing) it to the bot instead of posting the command in chat.
Note: your bot account needs a verified email and phone number on Twitch for whispers to work at all.
Remember each link's scan result for a w:
Remember each link's scan result for a while, so the same link posted again is answered from memory instead of costing another API call.
This is what keeps a raid affordable: thirty accounts pasting one link is one scan, not thirty. Every one of those messages is still deleted and still gets its notification - only the lookup is skipped.
Turn this off only if you want every single post re-scanned live.
How long a remembered scan result stays:
How long a remembered scan result stays usable before the link is scanned again.
Shorter means a site that gets compromised is re-checked sooner; longer means fewer API calls.
60 minutes is a good balance - a raid arrives inside a few minutes, so even a short window catches it, while an hour keeps a busy chat well inside the daily quota.
How many links in a single message Twitc:
How many links in a single message TwitchSentry will scan before it stops and ignores the rest.
Every scan costs one call against your API quota (VirusTotal's free tier allows 4 per minute and 500 per day), and a link the scanner has never seen before takes around 20 seconds to come back.
Without a cap, one message pasted full of links can spend the whole day's quota and hold up moderation while it works through them.
3 is plenty for real conversation. Raise it only if you genuinely expect people to post several links at once.
Rewrite links in the bot's own scan mess:
Rewrite links in the bot's own scan messages so they cannot be clicked - "example.com" is posted as "example[.]com".
The bot is a moderator, so nothing filters what it says. Repeating a malicious link back into chat, right after deleting the message that carried it, hands it out again from an account viewers trust.
Turn this off only if you would rather the links stayed clickable.
Post a message in chat when a scanned li: Post a message in chat when a scanned link comes back suspicious — not confirmed dangerous, but worth caution.
Post a message in chat when a scanned link comes back confirmed malicious.
Post a message in chat when a link is to: Post a message in chat when a link is too new/obscure for the scanning services to have any data on it yet.
Post a message in chat if a scan couldn': Post a message in chat if a scan couldn't finish for any reason (e.g. the scanning service was slow or unavailable).
Also scan links with IPQualityScore (IPQ: Also scan links with IPQualityScore (IPQS), in addition to VirusTotal, for a second opinion — especially good at catching brand-new/throwaway phishing domains.
Turn the whole Voting module on or off.
Post messages in chat about vote progres: Post messages in chat about vote progress (started, progress, result, etc.).
Ban the target of a successful vote inst: Ban the target of a successful vote instead of the default timeout.
Never let a vote succeed against one of: Never let a vote succeed against one of your subscribers.
Never let a vote succeed against someone: Never let a vote succeed against someone with the VIP badge.
Minimum account age in days before a use:
Minimum account age in days before a user is trusted.
Accounts younger than this value will receive a score hit.
(Example: 30 = accounts less than 30 days old are flagged)
How many emotes a message needs to have:
How many emotes a message needs to have before the emote-percentage check even looks at it.
Messages with fewer emotes than this are always ignored by that check, no matter what.
How many emotes in a row (with no words:
How many emotes in a row (with no words between them) it takes to count as spam.
Example: 5 = five or more emotes back-to-back adds to the score.
How many letters a message needs before:
How many letters a message needs before the caps-percentage check bothers looking at it.
Keeps short messages like "LOL" from ever being flagged just for being all caps.
How many times the exact same character:
How many times the exact same character has to repeat in a row to count as character spam.
Example: 6 = something like "AAAAAA" or "!!!!!!" (6 or more in a row) adds to the score.
Sliding time window in which a user's me:
Sliding time window in which a user's messages are counted.
(Example: 10 = only messages from the last 10 seconds count toward the velocity check)
Maximum number of messages a user may se:
Maximum number of messages a user may send within the window.
Sending more than this triggers a score hit.
(Example: 5 = the 6th message within the window triggers)
Sliding time window in which repeated me:
Sliding time window in which repeated messages are compared.
Older messages expire and no longer count as duplicates
Number of identical or similar messages:
Number of identical or similar messages (including the current one) within the window
required to trigger a score hit.
(Example: 3 = posting the same content a 3rd time triggers)
Minimum message length (letters/digits a:
Minimum message length (letters/digits after normalization) for the duplicate check.
Short messages like 'gg' or 'lol' are ignored — repeated short messages are still caught by the velocity check
How many DIFFERENT users must be among t:
How many DIFFERENT users must be among the counted violations before escalation may trigger.
This is what separates a spam wave from one annoying person: a single spammer is handled
by delete/timeout and should never put the whole chat into slow mode.
(Example: 2 = at least two different users must be involved, no matter how many violations one user racks up)
Sliding time window in which filtered vi:
Sliding time window in which filtered violations are counted toward escalation.
Violations older than this no longer count — so 'Violation Count' must be reached within this timespan.
(Example: 60 = five violations spread over ten minutes trigger nothing,
five violations within one minute trigger escalation)
Total number of filtered violations with:
Total number of filtered violations within the window required to trigger escalation.
Counts every violation the Message Filter acts on (caps, emotes, account age, flood), across all users.
Lower = reacts faster to small waves; higher = only reacts to sustained attacks.
(Example: 3 violations by 2 users within 60s = escalation triggers with default settings)
How long the activated chat mode stays o:
How long the activated chat mode stays on before it is lifted automatically.
Every renewed trigger during an active mode resets this timer to its full value,
so the protection stays up as long as the wave continues and ends on its own afterwards.
(Example: 300 = chat returns to normal 5 minutes after the last escalation trigger)
Seconds each user must wait between thei:
Seconds each user must wait between their own messages while slow mode is active.
This is Twitch's per-message delay — NOT how long the mode stays on (see 'Duration').
(Example: 10 = each user can post at most one message every 10 seconds)
Minimum follow age in minutes required t:
Minimum follow age in minutes required to chat while follower-only mode is active.
0 = following at all is enough. Higher values also lock out bots that follow
right before attacking.
(Example: 10 = anyone who followed less than 10 minutes ago cannot chat)
How long the raid protection stays armed:
How long the raid protection stays armed after an incoming raid.
After this duration the module goes back to sleep until the next raid
Only arm the protection for raids with a:
Only arm the protection for raids with at least this many viewers.
(Example: 0 = arm on every raid; 20 = ignore small friendly raids)
Sliding time window in which a user's me: Sliding time window in which a user's messages are counted during the raid window
Maximum number of messages a user may se:
Maximum number of messages a user may send within the window during a raid.
Stricter than the normal Flood Filter by default
Sliding time window in which repeated me: Sliding time window in which repeated messages of the same user are compared
Number of identical or similar messages:
Number of identical or similar messages from the same user within the window required to trigger.
(Example: 2 = the first repetition already triggers)
Minimum message length (letters/digits a:
Minimum message length (letters/digits after normalization) for the duplicate and swarm checks.
Shorter messages are only covered by the velocity check
Sliding time window in which messages fr: Sliding time window in which messages from different users are compared against each other
Number of distinct users posting near-id:
Number of distinct users posting near-identical messages within the window required to trigger.
(Example: 3 = as soon as a 3rd account posts the wave message, it is treated as a coordinated swarm)
Seconds each user must wait between mess:
Seconds each user must wait between messages while slow mode is active.
This is Twitch's per-message delay, not how long the mode stays on
Minimum follow age in minutes required t:
Minimum follow age in minutes required to chat while follower-only mode is active.
Higher values also lock out bots that followed shortly before the raid
How long (in seconds) a timeout lasts wh: How long (in seconds) a timeout lasts when "Action On Violation" above is set to Timeout. Example: 600 = 10 minutes.
How many emotes a message needs to have:
How many emotes a message needs to have before the emote-percentage check even looks at it.
Messages with fewer emotes than this are always ignored by that check.
How long (in seconds) a timeout lasts wh: How long (in seconds) a timeout lasts when "Action On Violation" above is set to Timeout. Example: 60 = 1 minute.
How many warnings a viewer can get befor:
How many warnings a viewer can get before the next one escalates into a timeout or ban.
Example: 2 = the 1st and 2nd violations are just warnings; the 3rd one escalates.
How long (in seconds) the escalation tim: How long (in seconds) the escalation timeout lasts. Example: 60 = 1 minute.
If a viewer goes this many hours without: If a viewer goes this many hours without another violation, their warning count resets back to zero — so a warning from weeks ago doesn't count against them forever.
How long (in seconds) a permit lasts by: How long (in seconds) a permit lasts by default when a moderator grants one. Example: 120 = 2 minutes.
The longest permit anyone can hand out. A moderator who types a longer time in "!Permit @user 3000" gets this instead, and so does a default or self-permit duration set above it.
This is what stops a mistyped duration from switching moderation off for someone for hours. Capped at 86400 (24 hours) whatever you put here.
Several viewers can hold a permit at the: Several viewers can hold a permit at the same time, each with its own countdown. A permit that is already running is never extended — !Permit for someone who already has one is refused, so end it with "!EndPermit @user" first. "!EndPermit" with no name ends every active permit at once.
Set the reward up on Twitch with \"Skip:
Set the reward up on Twitch with "Skip Reward Requests Queue" turned OFF. That is what lets TwitchSentry give the points back when a redemption cannot become a permit — the viewer already has one, or the feature is off. A reward that skips the queue is spent the moment it is redeemed and Twitch will not allow a refund.
Point the reward's Streamer.bot trigger at this same Permit action.
How long (in seconds) a self-granted per: How long (in seconds) a self-granted permit lasts. Example: 120 = 2 minutes.
How long (in hours) the learner keeps it:
How long (in hours) the learner keeps its downloaded list of common, everyday words (in many languages) before refreshing it. This list stops ordinary words like "the" or "und" from ever being suggested as spam.
Higher = fewer downloads. Lower = refreshes more often (rarely needed — this list barely changes).

How long (in hours) the learner keeps its downloaded list of valid domain endings (.com, .net, etc.) before refreshing it.
Higher = fewer downloads. Lower = refreshes more often (rarely needed).
How many DIFFERENT people need to have p:
How many DIFFERENT people need to have posted something before it can even become a suggestion.
This stops one repeat spammer from single-handedly teaching the learner a new rule — real spam campaigns usually involve more than one account.
The minimum \"confidence score\" somethi:
The minimum "confidence score" something needs before it's written down as a suggestion for you to review.
Confidence is a combined score based on how often it showed up, how many different messages and people it came from, and how spam-like the message around it looked.
The minimum confidence score a suggestio:
The minimum confidence score a suggestion needs to become "trusted" and be eligible for auto-promotion into spam.json.
Only matters if "Auto Promote Trusted Rules" above is turned on.
How many separate learner runs a suggest:
How many separate learner runs a suggestion has to keep reappearing in before it can be auto-promoted.
Makes sure it's a real, repeating pattern rather than a one-off fluke before it becomes an active rule.
The minimum number of times something ha:
The minimum number of times something has to show up (weighted) across recent violations before the learner even considers it.
This is just an early sanity check — it still has to clear the other requirements (how many messages, how many different people, and confidence) before actually becoming a suggestion.
The minimum number of separate violation:
The minimum number of separate violation-log entries something has to appear in before it can be suggested.
Stops a single, very repetitive spam message from teaching the learner a new rule all by itself.
Higher = more cautious/slower to react. Lower = reacts sooner, with less proof behind it.
The most single-word keyword suggestions:
The most single-word keyword suggestions the learner is allowed to add or refresh in one run.
A safety cap so a single busy run can't flood your suggestions list.
The most two-word phrase suggestions the:
The most two-word phrase suggestions the learner is allowed to add or refresh in one run.
Phrase suggestions tend to be more specific/precise than single-word keywords.
The most new domain-ending (TLD) suggest: The most new domain-ending (TLD) suggestions the learner is allowed to add or refresh in one run, based on spaced-out or disguised links it spotted.
How many of the most recent lines in vio:
How many of the most recent lines in violation-log.txt the learner reads through each time it looks for new patterns.
More lines = more history to learn from (usually more reliable results), but takes a little longer to process each run.
How much extra weight the message that j:
How much extra weight the message that just triggered this run gets, compared to older messages in the history.
Higher = the newest violation influences this run's results more strongly — but it still has to pass the same requirements as everything else before it can become a suggestion.
Controls how hard a word gets penalized:
Controls how hard a word gets penalized if it also shows up a lot in ordinary, non-violating chat (see "Clean-Chat Sample Rate" below).
Lower = stricter — everyday words that also appear in normal chat get suppressed more aggressively, which helps avoid false positives (like accidentally suggesting "google").
TwitchSentry saves roughly 1 out of ever:
TwitchSentry saves roughly 1 out of every N normal (non-violating) chat messages to clean-log.txt, to build up a sample of what everyday chat looks like — this feeds the Clean Penalty Divisor above.
Higher = samples less often and keeps the file smaller. Lower = builds the sample faster, but writes to disk more often.
The largest clean-log.txt is allowed to:
The largest clean-log.txt is allowed to grow (in kilobytes) before it's automatically trimmed down to just the most recent entries (see "History Lines" above).
Keeps this file from growing forever during long or very active streams.
How many separate learner runs a brand-n:
How many separate learner runs a brand-new suggestion has to keep appearing in before it's upgraded from "probation" to "trusted".
Higher = slower but safer. Lower = reacts faster, with less proof.
How many learner runs a pending suggesti:
How many learner runs a pending suggestion is allowed to go without reappearing before it's automatically removed from the suggestions list.
Gives suggestions some breathing room so a brief quiet spell doesn't wipe them out immediately.
How many of the most recent violation-lo: How many of the most recent violation-log entries are checked when deciding what still counts as "active" during cleanup.
How many times a rule or suggestion has:
How many times a rule or suggestion has to show up within that recent window to count as still active and be kept.
Higher = cleans up more aggressively. Lower = keeps rarely-used patterns around longer.
How strict Twitch's own AutoMod needs to:
How strict Twitch's own AutoMod needs to be before TwitchSentry acts on a held message. Twitch normally uses level 2 ("SmartDetection") as the baseline.
Goes from 1 to 4 — 4 is the strictest, but can start flagging (and then removing) messages you'd actually want to allow through.
IPQS rates every link on a scale from 0:
IPQS rates every link on a scale from 0 (totally safe) to 100 (certainly malicious). This is the minimum score at which TwitchSentry treats a link as a threat.
At 75, a link is considered suspicious (often a proxy, VPN exit node, or known bad actor).
IPQS's own guidance is 85 to outright block and 75 to flag for review — so 75 is the cautious, safer default.
Raise it toward 90 if you're seeing too many false alarms on your channel.
A lower, stricter version of the thresho:
A lower, stricter version of the threshold above, used only when IPQS also flags the domain as recently registered (i.e. a brand-new website).
Brand-new throwaway domains are a classic phishing trick — register one, use it once, then abandon it.
Since a new domain is inherently riskier, even a fraud score as low as 40 (normally considered "low risk") is enough to trigger a warning here.
Set this higher (e.g. 60-70) if you want to give new domains more benefit of the doubt.

TwitchSentry does not judge a message by: TwitchSentry does not judge a message by how many red flags it trips. It asks whether the message is built like an advertisement. An advert has parts: somewhere to go (Destination), something being sold (Offer), a way to redeem it (Instrument), the random @handle a spam bot signs with (Tag), and wording this channel has seen from spam before (Signature). One part on its own is a coincidence — plenty of ordinary messages have one. Two parts together is an advert. That is what these settings control.
Only act when a message contains at leas:
Only act when a message contains at least two different parts of an advert.
This is the single most important protection against deleting real conversation. "I got 100 followers today" is an Offer and nothing else, so it is left alone. "100 followers free, join discord.gg/x" is an Offer plus a Destination, so it is not.
A brand-new account is the one exception: one decisive part is enough for someone who has never spoken here before.
Turn off to let a single decisive part act on its own. Expect more false positives.
Skip the chat message when the sender is:
Skip the chat message when the sender is brand new AND the evidence was decisive — in other words, when it is plainly a bot.

A bot never reads the reply, so announcing every removal during a spam wave just doubles the noise in chat. The deletion, the Discord notification and the action log all still happen exactly as before; only the public message is skipped.

Turn off to always announce.
How many of the mentioned users have to:
How many of the mentioned users have to be real before the remaining @mentions are forgiven. Enter this as a fraction of 1 (0.5 = half of them).
"Real" means: seen chatting here recently, or (with "Verify Mentioned Users" on) an existing Twitch account. Example: 0.5 = someone greeting three regulars is left alone.
A randomly generated handle is never forgiven this way, no matter how many real people are mentioned alongside it. Set to 0 to switch forgiving off entirely.
How long someone counts as a \"known cha:
How long someone counts as a "known chatter" after their last message, in hours.
Mentions of users seen within this window are treated as real without any API lookup. Longer = more of your regulars are recognised, shorter = the list stays closer to who is actually around right now.
The total score a message needs to reach:
The total score a message needs to reach before TwitchSentry acts, on top of the two-parts rule above.
With the default part scores, two parts always add up to at least 1.50, so a threshold of 1.00 means the two-parts rule is what decides. Raise it towards 1.75 to additionally demand that one of those parts be a strong one.
Score for the part of an advert that say:
Score for the part of an advert that says WHERE to go: a disguised link ("streamboo .com", "dogehype dot com"), a known spam domain, an invite link, or a "search google for X" instruction.
Ordinary, well-formed links are not counted here at all — those belong to the Link Filter, and whitelisted domains are ignored entirely.
Score for the part that says WHAT is bei:
Score for the part that says WHAT is being sold: viewers, followers, primes, views — next to a price or a quantity ("cheap viewers", "10 Zuschauer kostenlos", "100 followers free").
Listing three different products at once, or repeating the same product phrase, counts as a strong Offer.
Score for the part that says HOW to rede:
Score for the part that says HOW to redeem it: a real redemption code ("GVP-8KJN-VM65-8QNG"), or a code word sitting next to a code-shaped word ("use promo code GROWTH20"), or an instruction like "remove the space".
Talking about codes without one present does not count — that is what keeps "anyone got a promo code for the sale?" safe.
Score for the random @handle a spam bot:
Score for the random @handle a spam bot signs its messages with — @rDsTUxjJ, @xY7zQw2L, @0af1Qc1R.
These are machine-generated: the capitalisation flips mid-word, there are almost no vowels, and digits sit between letters. Mentions of your regulars and of normal-looking names never count here.
Score for wording this channel has alrea:
Score for wording this channel has already seen from spam: an entry from your Strong Keywords list, or a match on one of your custom patterns.
This is the part that catches camouflaged spam like "uncontrollable grinning" or "chat explosions", which carries no link and no offer at all.
Score for a single everyday word from yo:
Score for a single everyday word from your keyword list — "cheap", "boost", "code" on its own.
Deliberately tiny, and these can never form a part of an advert by themselves. They only ever nudge a message that already has real evidence, so a keyword list full of common words cannot delete anything.
How many messages someone has to send he:
How many messages someone has to send here before they stop counting as brand new.
Brand-new accounts are the only ones a single decisive part of an advert can act on, which is what catches a bot's very first message.

How many messages someone has to send here before they count as a regular.
A regular is never actioned on circumstantial evidence: their message needs two parts AND at least one of them has to be decisive.
How much a regular's score is scaled dow:
How much a regular's score is scaled down. 0.8 = a regular needs 25% more evidence than a stranger for the same outcome.
Set to 1 to treat everyone the same regardless of history.
Messages shorter than this are judged on:
Messages shorter than this are judged on their evidence alone.
For longer messages TwitchSentry also asks how much of the text is actually the advert — one matching phrase buried in a long conversation is not a sales pitch.
How much of a long message has to be mad: How much of a long message has to be made up of evidence before it is treated as a full advert. Enter this as a fraction of 1 (0.2 = a fifth of the text).
How much to scale the score down when a:
How much to scale the score down when a long message falls under the coverage ratio above. 0.75 = knock a quarter off.
This can only ever lower a score, never raise one.
How many different clean messages a word:
How many different clean messages a word has to appear in before TwitchSentry treats it as an ordinary word for your channel.
This list builds itself from your own chat, which is how third-party emote names (7TV, BTTV, FFZ) and in-jokes stop being mistaken for disguised spam without you listing them anywhere.
The sites viewer-bot spam sends people t:
The sites viewer-bot spam sends people to — "streamboo", "dogehype", "nezhna". Just the name, no ".com" needed. One per line.
These are recognised however they are written: as a real link, spaced out ("streamboo .com"), spelled out ("dogehype dot com") or hidden behind lookalike characters. A message naming one of these counts as a decisive Destination.
This is the list the Spam Learner is best at filling — it reads the domains straight out of the spam it sees.
Wording that points at an advert. Multi-:
Wording that points at an advert. Multi-word entries ("cheap viewers", "promo code") are the useful ones — they get sorted into the part of an advert they describe. One entry per line.
A single everyday word here ("cheap", "boost", "code") is only ever a small nudge and can never delete a message by itself, so a loose list cannot cause false positives.
Start an entry with "!" (e.g. "!scamword") to protect it from the Spam Learner's cleanup.
Wording that never turns up in real chat:
Wording that never turns up in real chat — spam signature phrases like "uncontrollable grinning", "chat explosions", "viewers snoring". One per line.
These count as a decisive Signature, which is what catches camouflaged spam carrying no link and no offer at all. A message still needs a second part of an advert before anything happens, unless the sender is brand new.
Put site names in "Spam Domains" above rather than here.
Posted in chat when a message is deleted:
Posted in chat when a message is deleted for being spam.

This is the fallback. If you fill in one of the six situation messages below, that one is used instead — leave them empty and everything comes through here.
A different sentence depending on what w:
A different sentence depending on what was actually found, instead of one message for everything. Whichever fits is used when a message is deleted; leave one empty and it falls back to the Remove Message above.

When several apply at once, the most explanatory one wins: disguised characters first, then advertising link, promo code, offer, wording, and bot mention last. Use {categories} if you want the message to name the others too.
Used when the message pointed somewhere:: Used when the message pointed somewhere: a disguised link ("streamboo .com", "dogehype dot com"), a known spam site, an invite link, or a "search google for X" instruction.
Used when the message was selling someth: Used when the message was selling something — viewers, followers, primes, views — next to a price or a quantity.
Used when the message carried a redempti: Used when the message carried a redemption code, or a code word sitting next to a code-shaped word.
Used when the message tagged a randomly:
Used when the message tagged a randomly generated @handle — the signature a spam bot leaves behind.

Note this rarely wins on its own: a bot handle almost always turns up alongside a link or an offer, and those explain the removal better. Add {categories} to any of these messages if you want the mention named as well.
Used when the message matched your Stron: Used when the message matched your Strong Keywords or one of your custom patterns — the camouflaged spam that carries no link and no offer at all.
Used when lookalike characters were hidi:
Used when lookalike characters were hiding a word that would otherwise have matched — "Ch͡eap vie̮wers".

This one outranks all the others, because it is the clearest thing you can tell somebody about why their message went.
The short phrases that fill {reason}. Ke: The short phrases that fill {reason}. Keep them as fragments that read naturally inside a sentence — they are dropped straight into your timeout and ban wording, and into any message using {reason}.
Fills {reason} when the message pointed: Fills {reason} when the message pointed to an advertising site.
Fills {reason} when the message was sell: Fills {reason} when the message was selling viewers, followers or similar.
Fills {reason} when the message carried: Fills {reason} when the message carried a redemption or promo code.
Fills {reason} when the message tagged a: Fills {reason} when the message tagged a randomly generated bot handle.
Fills {reason} when the message matched: Fills {reason} when the message matched wording already known from spam.
Fills {reason} when lookalike characters: Fills {reason} when lookalike characters were hiding a word.
Fills {reason} in the rare case where no: Fills {reason} in the rare case where nothing more specific applies.

Select a suggestion to inspect details.
New spam sites, wording and domain-endin: New spam sites, wording and domain-endings the Spam Learner has spotted but not added to the real block list yet. Read the "Would hit" column first: that is how many real messages from your own clean log this rule would have matched. Zero is what you want, and anything above zero is never auto-promoted — those rows are sorted to the top so you see them first. Users = how many different people posted it (one spammer repeating himself counts once). Docs = how many separate messages it appeared in. Discrim. = how much more often it shows up in spam than in ordinary chat. Confidence combines all of that. Status "probation" means it is still building a track record; "trusted" means it is proven enough to be auto-promoted, if that is turned on in Learner settings. Click a row to see what it would do and where it would land.
